issues.legal_issue: An announced incentive contained in operative rules may support promissory estoppel when an entrepreneur makes substantial investments in reliance on it, and a draft amendment alone does not displace the operative rules.
material_facts: The State had an industrial policy providing sales-tax incentives for eligible industries, and the operative rules provided for those incentives without listing the relevant industries as excluded.

Before the final amendment, the entrepreneurs invested substantial amounts and took steps toward establishing or expanding their industrial units, including obtaining permissions and entering into installation or licensing arrangements.
The State had published a draft amendment, but the final amendment had not yet taken effect during the period in which the entrepreneurs made those investments and took those steps.

The final amendment added the relevant industry to the excluded list and included a transitional note recognizing benefits for qualifying investment made before the amendment; that note was later omitted with retrospective effect.
issues.conclusion: The draft amendment did not displace the operative rules, and the entrepreneurs’ reliance and substantial steps could not be disregarded in deciding their claims. The High Court’s judgment was set aside, and the claims were remitted for fresh consideration; the Court did not decide the quantum or ultimate extent of any exemption.
issues.legal_principle: Promissory estoppel can operate against the State in the legislative field, subject to equity and public interest. A clear representation and reliance causing a change of position must be established. Draft rules cannot be treated as operative amendments while existing rules govern the field. The Court relied on Collector of Bombay v. Municipal Corporation of the City of Bombay, Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Pournami Oil Mills v. State of Kerala, Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes v. Dharmendra Trading Company, Mangalore Chemicals and Fertilisers Ltd. v. Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, Pawan Alloys & Casting Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P. State Electricity Board, State of Punjab v. Nestle India Ltd., State of Rajasthan v. J.K. Udaipur Udyog Ltd., Bannari Amman Sugars Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer, and Union of India v. V. Ramakrishnan.

rule.if: incentive_claim_appeal and incentive_rules_were_operative and entrepreneurs_invested_in_reliance and draft_change_was_not_final

predicates.incentive_claim_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning the denial of an industrial incentive claim.
predicates.incentive_rules_were_operative: The State had rules providing the incentive in force when the entrepreneurs acted.
predicates.entrepreneurs_invested_in_reliance: The entrepreneurs made substantial investments or took material steps to establish or expand their units in reliance on the incentive representation.
predicates.draft_change_was_not_final: The proposed change had been published only as a draft and had not yet become a final amendment when the entrepreneurs acted.

issues.definition: When an incentive claim appeal concerns entrepreneurs who relied on operative incentive rules and invested before a proposed amendment became final, the draft change does not displace their reliance-based claim.

issues.legal_issue: A retrospective amendment to subordinate legislation cannot remove rights conferred under existing rules unless the parent statute authorizes retrospective rule-making at the time of the amendment.
material_facts: A transitional note in the rules recognized sales-tax benefits for qualifying investment made before the relevant industry was added to the excluded list.
The note was later omitted with purported retrospective effect, before the parent statute expressly authorized retrospective rule-making for the relevant rules.
The entrepreneurs relied on the existing rules and the transitional note, and the Court found that rights had been conferred under the note.
issues.conclusion: The amendments made before the parent statute authorized retrospective rule-making could not retrospectively take away the entrepreneurs’ rights under the transitional note.
issues.legal_principle: Subordinate legislation may operate retrospectively only when the parent statute confers that power. A statute is not construed to have retrospective operation unless that construction is clear from its terms or follows by necessary and distinct implication. The Court relied on Section 64(2A) of the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973, and West v. Gwynne, and held that the relevant retrospective rule-making power became available only after Section 64(2A) came into force. A delegatee may make rules only within the limits of the parent statute.

predicates.subordinate_rule_challenge: The proceeding challenges a retrospective change to a rule made under delegated legislative authority.
predicates.accrued_incentive_right_under_existing_r: An existing rule conferred an incentive-related right on the affected person before the change.
predicates.parent_law_lacked_retrospective_rulemaki: The parent law did not authorize retrospective rule-making when the amendment was made.

issues.definition: A retrospective change to a subordinate rule cannot remove an accrued incentive right when the parent law did not authorize retrospective rule-making at the time of the change.
